title: Tax Laws Amendment (2008 Measures No. 1) Bill 2008

divisions.question: That this bill be now read a second time. That the words proposed to be omitted ( **Mr Keenan’s** amendment) stand part of the question.
That the amendments ( **Senator Milne’s** ) be agreed to.
That this bill be now read a third time.

speeches.speaker: John Faulkner
speeches.brief: The bills were introduced together, and a motion to allow them to proceed without formalities and be read a first time was agreed to.

speeches.speaker: John Faulkner
speeches.brief: The government sought $3.3 billion in additional appropriations through two bills, including $2.4 billion for departmental programs and $898.5 million for payments to states and non-operating expenses, while announcing savings of around $100 million in 2007-08 from a two per cent efficiency dividend and $15.4 million from a 30 per cent reduction in ministerial and opposition staff. It also introduced bills to increase utilities allowance to $500 per year for pensioners, carers, and people with disability, expand VET FEE-HELP loans to high-level vocational courses, and remove tax deductibility for political donations.

speeches.speaker: Helen Coonan
speeches.brief: The opposition argued that ending tax-deductibility for political donations (schedule 1 of the bill) would harm small individual donors while leaving union and corporate donations unaffected, and that the Labor government was using the change for political advantage. The coalition opposed the measure, citing a biased committee report and estimated budget savings of $31.4 million over four years.

speeches.speaker: Christine Milne
speeches.brief: The senator criticised the government for inserting carbon sink forest provisions into a separate tax bill without notifying the Senate, and announced an amendment to the now-passed legislation. They argued the scheme would distort agricultural land markets, displace farmers—citing Tully cane growers and Preolenna in Tasmania—and fail to ensure permanent carbon storage, urging protection of existing carbon stores instead.

speeches.speaker: Christine Milne
speeches.brief: Senator Milne argued the bill’s tax deductions for plantation carbon sinks lacked requirements for biodiversity, hydrological assessment, or minimum timeframes, costing $25.3 million in forgone revenue over three years while subsidising plantations that could replace food production and native forests. Senator Ronaldson opposed removing tax-deductibility for political donations, arguing the government was cherry‑picking reform due to the Wollongong scandal and that Treasury could not justify the claimed $10 million annual savings. Senator Brown and Senator Heffernan also criticised the plantation provisions as a rort that could allow tax deductions even if trees died or burned.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Conroy
speeches.brief: The speaker tabled government amendments to replace "gift-deductible entity" with "concessional entity" in the GST Act and to remove schedules 2 to 6 from the bill, arguing the changes were needed to pass beneficial tax measures before the end of the income year. The speaker also opposed a Greens amendment on carbon sink forests, calling it unworkable, while other senators argued the bill's carbon sink provisions were fundamentally flawed and risked creating a tax rort.

speeches.speaker: Claire Moore
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Tax Laws Amendment (2008 Measures No. 1) Bill 2008 lacks any requirement for carbon sink forests to remain standing, allowing investors to claim up‑front tax deductions and then cut down trees after 15 years for further deductions, constituting a tax avoidance scheme. They supported Senator Milne’s amendment mandating trees be kept for at least 100 years and warned the bill would drive large corporations onto prime agricultural land, repeating the harms of managed investment schemes.

speeches.speaker: Steve Hutchins
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the bill allows tax deductions for carbon sink forests with no requirement to keep trees in the ground, enabling industries to double-dip by also harvesting timber, and warned it will drive farmers off prime agricultural land and destroy rural communities like King Island. They called for the bill to be rejected or subjected to a Senate inquiry, criticising the government for failing to provide environmental guidelines.

speeches.speaker: Gavin Marshall
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the carbon sink provisions in the Tax Laws Amendment Bill are a rort benefiting coal and forestry industries, and supported Senator Milne's amendment requiring trees to be planted for at least 100 years. He criticised the government for lacking guidelines and failing to disclose whether trees can be cut down, and noted the bill would forgo $24.3 million in revenue over three years.

speeches.speaker: John Hogg
speeches.brief: The speaker warned that the carbon sink forest tax deduction scheme could be rendered unworkable by a disallowable instrument, and that no formal socioeconomic study had been conducted on its impacts. The government estimated 80,500 hectares would be planted by 2011 based on the voluntary carbon market, but the environmental guidelines had not yet been tabled.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Conroy
speeches.brief: A motion was carried to refer the implementation, operation and administration of Carbon Sink Forests legislation to the Rural and Regional Affairs and Transport Committee for inquiry and report by 22 August 2008, with the effect that further consideration of the bill would resume on the first sitting day after the committee reports.
